blocks.text: The turtledove is called תור thor in Hebrew and τρυγών [trygōn] in Greek. These names, however [col. 55] similar, are not derived from one another but are onomatopoeic (ὀνοματοποιητικά [onomatopoiētika]). They were formed, that is, in imitation of the song of the turtledove, which in Greek is called τρυσμὸς [trysmos], from the verb τρύζειν [tryzein], that is, to moan in the manner of a turtledove. So Pollux, book 5, ch. 14, in the section On the calls of birds: Εἴποις δ' ἂν τρυγόνας τρύζειν, περιστερὰς γογγύζειν [Eipois d' an trygonas tryzein, peristeras gongyzein]. But for Suidas and the Etymologicum, too, τρύζειν [tryzein] is ψιθυρίζειν, γογγύζειν, ἀσήμως λαλεῖν παρὰ καὶ ἡ τρυγὼν, ἐπεὶ καὶ ἀσήμως φθέγγεται καὶ γογγυστικῶς [psithyrizein, gongyzein, asēmōs lalein para kai hē trygōn, epei kai asēmōs phthengetai kai gongystikōs], to whisper, to murmur, to speak indistinctly, like the turtledove too, because it sings indistinctly and with a murmur. Hence Clement, in the fifth book of the Stromata: Γογγύζουσα ἡ τρυγὼν, μέμψεως καταλαλιὰν ἀχάριστον ἐμφαίνουσα, εἰκότως ἐξοικίζεται [Gongyzousa hē trygōn, mempseōs katalalian acharistōn emphainousa, eikotōs exoikizetai]. The murmuring turtledove, displaying the ungrateful slander of complaint, is rightly driven from the house. For others τρύζειν [tryzein] is πολυφωνεῖν, καὶ πολυλογεῖν [polyphōnein, kai polylogein], to chatter a great deal. Because τὴν τρυγόνα ἡ παροιμία ἐπὶ σκώμματι τῶν πολυλογούντων παραλαμβάνει, λαλιστέρους τῶν τρυγόνων τοιούτους καλοῦσα [tēn trygona hē paroimia epi skōmmati tōn polylogountōn paralambanei, lalisterous tōn trygonōn toioutous kalousa], the proverb uses the turtledove to mock those who chatter a great deal, calling them more talkative than turtledoves. So Eustathius, on that line of Homer, Iliad 1, verse 31:
Ὡς μή μοι τρύζητε παρήμενοι ἄλλοθεν ἄλλος, [Hōs mē moi tryzēte parēmenoi allothen allos,]

So that you may not chatter at me, sitting by, one from here, another from there. Besides the paroemiographers, the proverb is mentioned by Alexis in the Thraso in Athenaeus, book 4; by Menander in the Plocium; by Demetrius in the Sicilia in Aelian, On Animals, book 12, chapter 12; and by Clement in the first book of the Stromata. To this belongs what is said of chattering women in Theocritus' Syracusan Women:
Τρυγόνες ἐκκναισεῦντι πλατυάσδοισαι ἅπαντα, [Trygones ekknaiseunti platyasdoisai hapanta,]

Like turtledoves they deafen us, broadening their mouths on every word. Nor do I approve the proposal of a great man to read ἐκ Ναύσοιο [ek Nausoio], that is, from the island of Sicily, instead of ἐκκναισεῦντι [ekknaiseunti]. Ναῦσος [Nausos], he says, like Νᾶσος [Nasos], is a word of the Dorians and the Sicilians, who so called their Sicily. The poet therefore very wittily calls the Dorian-speaking women (τοὺς Δωριζούσας [tous Dōrizousas]), who pronounce everything with a broad mouth, τρυγόνας ἐκ [II, 597] Ναύσοιο [trygonas ek Nausoio]. This conjecture, I say, I do not approve, because there is no need to change anything, since the received reading yields a most fitting sense. Ἐκκναίειν [Ekknaiein] means to deafen the ears, like ἀποκναίειν [apoknaiein]. Pollux: Ἀποκναίων ἀηδίᾳ, κόπτων τὰ ὦτα [Apoknaiōn aēdia, koptōn ta ōta], ἀποκναίων [apoknaiōn] by his unpleasantness, or by his inanities, that is, deafening the ears. As Demosthenes wrote against Midias, p. 362: Ἀποκναίει γὰρ ἀηδίᾳ, δήπου καὶ ἀναιθησίᾳ καθ᾽ ἑκάστην τὴν ἐκκλησίαν ταῦτα λέγων· [Apoknaiei gar aēdia, dēpou kai anaithēsia kath' hekastēn tēn ekklēsian tauta legōn;] For he deafens us with his inanities and stupidity, hammering the same things in at every assembly. Thus, then, it is said of chatterboxes, Τρυγόνες ἐκκναισεῦντι [Trygones ekknaiseunti], Doric for ἐκκναίσουσι [ekknaisousi], Turtledoves (or like turtledoves) deafen the ears with their talkativeness. Among the Proverbs in Suidas there is Τρυγόνα ψάλλειν [Trygona psallein], To sing the turtledove, ἐπὶ τῶν φαύλως πραττων [epi tōn phaulōs prattōn], said of those who do something badly, because the voice of the turtledove is utterly unmusical. And perhaps this is why it is called צלצל by the Hebrews, צרצילתא by the Chaldeans, and in Arabic also صلصل [ṣalṣal], as if the name were formed from a cymbal, because it has a ringing and noisy voice. Indeed, if we believe Gesner, for this very reason a species of cicada, the cercope, is compared with the turtledove in these words of Athenaeus, book 4, ch. 4: Ἔστι δ᾽ ἡ κερκώπη ζῶον ὅμοιον τέττιγι, καὶ τρυγονίῳ· [Esti d' hē kerkōpē zōon homoion tettigi, kai trygoniō;] The cercope is an animal like a cicada and a turtledove. On these words he says: The cercope resembles the turtledove in nothing else than its noisy chatter. But Dale- [col. 56] champius conjectures that a cricket is so called from the peculiarity of the sound tri. And the great Casaubon passed over this passage unconcerned. Yet that it is corrupt is as certain as whatever is most certain, and τρυγονίῳ [trygoniō] is wrongly read for τεττιγονίῳ [tettigoniō], which is a species of cicada. Aristotle, Hist. book 5, ch. 30: Καλοῦσι δέ τινες τοὺς μὲν μεγάλους (τῶν τεττίγων) καὶ ᾄδοντας ἄχετας· τοὺς δὲ μικροὺς τεττιγόνια [Kalousi de tines tous men megalous (tōn tettigōn) kai adontas achetas; tous de mikrous tettigonia]. Hence Pliny, book 11, ch. 26: Those that sing are called achetae, and the smaller of them tettigonia. So this passage contains nothing that can be referred to the chattering of turtledoves. That chattering, though often annoying, nevertheless has something pleasing: it signals that spring and summer have come, since turtledoves do not appear in winter. Hence it is said in Cant. II, 11. 12.: For now the winter is past, the rain is over and gone. Flowers are seen on the earth. The time of song has come, and the voice of the turtledove is heard in our land. And Ierem. VIII, 7.: The turtledove and the swallow and the crane have observed the time of their coming. For the turtledove is a migratory bird ^{(1)}. Aristotle, Hist. book 8, ch. 3.
